question: On a lab test rig, acceleration follows a(t) = 2t² + 3t (in m/s², t in seconds); the speed gained between t = 2 s and t = 3 s, from the area under this graph, is tripled. This total speed belongs to a 4 kg slider. A separate stopwatch reads 20 seconds, unrelated to this task. From the resulting kinetic energy, 6 J is subtracted, and the total is converted into kilojoules. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

On a crane test rig, two acceleration readings, in m/s², sum to 9 and multiply to 8; the larger is kept as the acceleration acting on a load whose mass is 168 kg. From the resulting force, 8 N is subtracted. A separate voltmeter reads 3 V, unrelated to this task. The force is converted into kilonewtons, and finally reduced by 2 kN. What is the final force, in kilonewtons?

A lab's final energy reading, in kilojoules after a last addition of 28 kJ, is wanted — but it starts with two rod lengths. Two rods measure 104 cm and 333 cm; the greatest length dividing both evenly is used as the speed, in meters per second, of a 4 kg slider. The slider's kinetic energy is scaled by a factor of 12, converted into kilojoules, scaled again by a factor of 11, and finally increased by 28 kJ. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

Two rods measure 226 cm and 197 cm; the greatest length dividing both evenly is used as the acceleration, in m/s², of a machine part whose mass is stated as 128000 grams. A separate voltmeter reads 7 V, unrelated to this task. The resulting force is converted into kilonewtons, then reduced by 17 kN, then scaled by a factor of 3, and finally scaled again by a factor of 3. What is the final force, in kilonewtons?

On a lab test bench, two speeds, in m/s, sum to 11 and multiply to 24; the smaller is kept, multiplied by 8, and then 19 m/s is added. This total speed belongs to a slider whose mass is stated as 38 kg. A separate voltmeter reads 4 V, unrelated to this task. The slider's kinetic energy is converted into kilojoules, and finally scaled by a factor of 10. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

A crane's final force reading, in kilonewtons after a last addition of 20 kN, is wanted — but it starts with a set of test modules. From 9 interchangeable modules, engineers select groups of 3 for a load trial; the number of distinct such groups has 5 subtracted from it. This total, used as an acceleration in m/s², acts on a load whose mass is stated as 176000 grams. To the resulting force, 30 N is added, and the total is converted into kilonewtons. Finally, 20 kN is added. What is the final force, in kilonewtons?

From 12 interchangeable modules on a lab bench, engineers select groups of 2 for a diagnostic test; the number of distinct such groups is used as the speed, in meters per second, of a slider whose mass is stated as 56000 grams. A separate stopwatch reads 38 seconds, unrelated to this task. The slider's kinetic energy is converted into kilojoules, increased by 21 kJ, and finally doubled. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

A machine's final force reading, in newtons after a last subtraction of 24 N, is wanted — but it starts with two rod lengths. Two rods measure 171 cm and 365 cm; the greatest length dividing both evenly is found, multiplied by 7, and then 16 is added. This total, used as an acceleration in m/s², acts on a part whose mass is stated as 63000 grams. Finally, from the resulting force, 24 N is subtracted. What is the final force, in newtons?

A crane's final force reading, in kilonewtons after two successive additions, is wanted — but it starts with two acceleration readings. Two readings, in m/s², sum to 9 and multiply to 14; the smaller is kept as the acceleration acting on a load whose mass is stated as 85000 grams. From the resulting force, 30 N is subtracted, and the total is converted into kilonewtons. A separate voltmeter reads 9 V, unrelated to this task. Finally, 14 kN is added, then 29 kN is added again. What is the final force, in kilonewtons?

On a lab test bench, two speed values, in m/s, sum to 10 and multiply to 16; the larger is kept as the speed of a slider whose mass is stated as 37000 grams. The slider's kinetic energy is scaled by a factor of 6, scaled again by 5, then reduced by 23 J, and finally reduced once more by 4 J. What is the final energy, in joules?

A machine's final force reading, in newtons after a last sevenfold scaling, is wanted — but it starts with a batch of test modules. From 6 interchangeable modules, engineers select groups of 3 for a stress test; the number of distinct such groups is used as the acceleration, in m/s², of a part whose mass is 72 kg. A separate thermometer reads 30°C, unrelated to this task. The resulting force is scaled by a factor of 11, scaled again by 12, and finally scaled once more by 7. What is the final force, in newtons?

A lab's final energy reading, in kilojoules, is wanted after one last conversion — but it starts with an acceleration profile. On a test cart, acceleration follows a(t) = 5t² + 3t (in m/s², t in seconds) from a standstill; the speed gained between t = 0 s and t = 2 s, from the area under this graph, belongs to a cart whose mass is stated as 21000 grams. The cart's kinetic energy is scaled by a factor of 8, scaled again by 8, and finally converted into kilojoules. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

A lab's final energy reading, in kilojoules after three successive adjustments, is wanted — but it starts with two speed readings. Two speeds of 6 m/s and 8 m/s are added and the sum multiplied by 3, giving the effective speed of a slider whose mass is stated as 18000 grams. The slider's kinetic energy is converted into kilojoules, then increased by 12 kJ, reduced by 24 kJ, and reduced once more by 19 kJ. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

From 13 interchangeable modules on a lab bench, engineers select groups of 2 for a durability test; the number of distinct such groups is used as the speed, in meters per second, of a slider whose mass is stated as 5000 grams. From the resulting kinetic energy, 15 J is added, and the total is scaled by a factor of 3. The result is converted into kilojoules, and finally scaled once more by a factor of 10. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

On a lab test bench, two rods measure 28 cm and 188 cm; the greatest length dividing both evenly is used as the speed, in meters per second, of a slider whose mass is stated as 11000 grams. A separate voltmeter reads 6 V, unrelated to this task. The slider's kinetic energy is scaled by a factor of 4, scaled again by 8, then reduced by 22 J, and finally converted into kilojoules. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

On a lab test bench, two speeds of 6 m/s and 5 m/s are added and the sum multiplied by 3, giving the effective speed of a slider whose mass is stated as 14 kg. A separate thermometer reads 27°C, unrelated to this task. The slider's kinetic energy is scaled by a factor of 5, scaled again by 5, scaled once more by 6, and finally converted into kilojoules. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

A lab's final energy reading, in kilojoules after a final tenfold scaling, is wanted — but it starts with an acceleration profile. On a test cart, acceleration follows a(t) = t² + 5t (in m/s², t in seconds) from a standstill; the speed gained between t = 0 s and t = 4 s, from the area under this graph, belongs to a cart whose mass is stated as 47000 grams. From the resulting kinetic energy, 18 J is subtracted, and the total is converted into kilojoules. A separate stopwatch reads 42 seconds, unrelated to this task. Then 23 kJ is subtracted, and finally the total is scaled by a factor of 10. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

A machine's final force reading, in newtons after a last addition of 10 N, is wanted — but it starts with two acceleration readings. Two readings, in m/s², sum to 11 and multiply to 24; the smaller is kept, then multiplied by 11. This total acceleration acts on a part whose mass is 127 kg. The resulting force is scaled by a factor of 5, and finally 10 N is added. What is the final force, in newtons?

A lab's final energy reading, in kilojoules after a final ninefold scaling, is wanted — but it starts with an acceleration profile. On a test cart, acceleration follows a(t) = 2t² + 7t (in m/s², t in seconds) from a standstill; the speed gained between t = 0 s and t = 2 s has 7 m/s subtracted from it. This net speed belongs to a cart whose mass is stated as 41000 grams. From the resulting kinetic energy, 14 J is subtracted, the total is converted into kilojoules, and finally scaled by a factor of 9. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

On a hydraulic press, the rate at which the ram's acceleration changes follows j(t) = 2t² + 6t (in m/s³, t in seconds); between t = 1 s and t = 2 s, the net change in acceleration acts on a ram whose mass is 69 kg. A separate stopwatch reads 25 seconds, unrelated to this task. The resulting force is converted into kilonewtons, then reduced by 15 kN, and reduced again by 15 kN. What is the final force, in kilonewtons?

A machine's final force reading, in newtons after a last subtraction of 24 N, is wanted — but it starts with two acceleration readings. Two readings, in m/s², sum to 4 and multiply to 3; the smaller is kept, then multiplied by 7. This total acceleration acts on a part whose mass is stated as 139000 grams. The resulting force is scaled by a factor of 4, and finally reduced by 24 N. What is the final force, in newtons?

A lab's final energy reading, in kilojoules after a final doubling, is wanted — but it starts with an acceleration profile. On a test cart, acceleration follows a(t) = 4t² + 6t (in m/s², t in seconds); the speed gained between t = 1 s and t = 3 s belongs to a cart whose mass is stated as 51000 grams. The cart's kinetic energy is converted into kilojoules, scaled by a factor of 9, scaled again by 10, and finally doubled. What is the final energy, in kilojoules?

On a lab test cart, acceleration follows a(t) = 3t² + 2t (in m/s², t in seconds) from a standstill; the speed gained between t = 0 s and t = 3 s belongs to a 19 kg cart. From the cart's kinetic energy, 26 J is subtracted, then 13 J is added back, the total is scaled by a factor of 11, and finally 6 J is added. What is the final energy, in joules?

A machine's final force reading, in newtons after a last sixfold scaling, is wanted — but it starts with two acceleration readings. Two readings, in m/s², sum to 7 and multiply to 12; the larger is kept, 13 m/s² is added, and the total is multiplied by 4. This acceleration acts on a part whose mass is 101 kg. From the resulting force, 3 N is subtracted, and finally the total is scaled by a factor of 6. What is the final force, in newtons?

On a crane test rig, two cables measure 154 cm and 31 cm; the greatest length dividing both evenly is used as the acceleration, in m/s², of a load whose mass is 25 kg. The resulting force is converted into kilonewtons, then reduced by 5 kN, increased by 8 kN, and finally reduced once more by 9 kN. What is the final force, in kilonewtons?
